assessment.name: Year 8 Art and D&T Autumn assessment

units.name: The 6 Rs and the product life cycle
Art: Sarah Graham and the formal elements

leitner_plan.new: 6 Rs, life cycle and designing for a client (5)

leitner_plan.quiz: DT5 and DT6 quizzes, draw two letters in isometric

cards.title: The 6 Rs (part 1): reduce, reuse, recycle
cards.question: What do reduce, reuse and recycle mean in design?
points: Reduce: decrease the number of materials needed to make a product. Example: using pre-cut materials to minimise waste.
Reuse: think of another use for a product before throwing it away. Example: using a clean, empty food tin as a pen pot.
Recycle: make sure products are converted back to their basic materials. Example: recycling plastic with other plastic.
These reduce waste and help protect the environment.
cards.watch_out: Reuse keeps the product in the same form for a new job; recycle breaks it down into raw material first.
cards.hook: Reduce = less. Reuse = again. Recycle = remake.
cards.grade9: Suggest how to minimise waste when making a lamp: plan the cutting layout so pieces fit together tightly.

cards.title: The 6 Rs (part 2): refuse, repair, rethink
cards.question: What do refuse, repair and rethink mean in design?
points: Refuse: decide not to buy products that could harm the environment. Example: not buying a plastic bag.
Repair: mend broken products instead of throwing them away. Example: getting a phone repaired instead of buying a new one.
Rethink: decide whether we need a product before we buy it. Example: choosing a reusable bag instead of a plastic one.
Together with reduce, reuse and recycle these make the 6 Rs of sustainable design.
cards.watch_out: Refuse means saying no to a harmful product; rethink means thinking about a better choice. They are close but not the same.
cards.hook: All 6 Rs: Reduce, Reuse, Recycle, Refuse, Repair, Rethink.
cards.grade9: Compare reuse and repair: both keep a product out of the bin, but repair fixes it for its original job, while reuse gives it a new job.

cards.title: Product life cycle
cards.question: What are the original source, manufacture and disposal of a product?
points: Original source: where the material comes from. Example: timber comes from wood, and the original source of wood is trees.
Manufacture: how the product is made, by hand with hand tools, or designed on a computer and made by a machine such as a 3D printer or laser cutter.
Disposal: how the product is got rid of at the end of its life, such as recycling or reusing.
A lamp made of wood, paper and electronics should be separated so each part can be recycled properly.
cards.watch_out: Electronics must not go in the normal bin. They are taken to an electrical recycling point.
cards.grade9: Explain why separating materials matters: recycling only works when the same materials are put together.

cards.title: Design brief, client profile, needs and wants
cards.question: What are a design brief, a client profile, needs and wants?
points: Design brief: a document that outlines the core details and expectations of a design project. Example: design a personalised tote bag inspired by Keith Haring.
Client profile: a summary of the client's likes and dislikes, such as their favourite colour.
Needs: characteristics the design must have. Example: a phone case must fit an iPhone 13.
Wants: characteristics the client would like. Example: red and blue geometric shapes.
cards.watch_out: Needs are must haves; wants are nice to haves. A product that misses a need has failed the brief.
cards.hook: Need it, or it fails. Want it, it is a bonus.
cards.grade9: When designing for a brief, label each feature as meeting a need or a want.

cards.title: Primary and secondary data, geometric and organic shapes
cards.question: What are primary and secondary data, and geometric and organic shapes?
points: Primary data: gathered directly from a client. Example: asking someone to fill in a questionnaire.
Secondary data: gathered from another source. Example: data from the internet or a book.
Geometric shapes are mathematically accurate. 2D: triangle, square, circle. 3D: pyramid, cube, sphere.
Organic shapes do not follow mathematical rules, like leaves or clouds. They are hard to copy exactly in 3D.
cards.watch_out: Primary means first hand from the client; secondary means someone else already collected it.
cards.grade9: Explain which data is more useful for a personalised product: primary, because it tells you exactly what this client wants.

cards.title: Hardwoods, softwoods and manufactured boards
cards.question: What are hardwoods, softwoods and manufactured boards?
points: Hardwoods come from deciduous trees, with flat leaves that shed every autumn. Examples: oak, birch, ash, mahogany, balsa.
Softwoods come from coniferous trees, with thin needle leaves that stay green all year. Examples: pine, larch, spruce.
Manufactured boards are made from recycled wood fibres or layers glued together. Examples: MDF, plywood, chipboard.
MDF (medium density fibreboard) is made by breaking wood into fibres, mixing them with glue, then pressing them into flat sheets.
cards.watch_out: Balsa is a hardwood even though it is very soft and light. Hardwood is about the tree type.
cards.hook: Hardwood trees drop their leaves (deciduous); softwood trees keep their needles (coniferous).
cards.grade9: Explain why manufactured boards are useful: they come in large flat sheets and use waste wood.

cards.title: Renewable and non renewable resources
cards.question: What is the difference between renewable and non renewable resources?
points: A renewable resource is sourced naturally, such as wood from trees. It will never run out if it is managed properly, for example by replanting.
Renewable materials like wood are biodegradable, so they break down naturally.
A non renewable resource, such as metal ore from the ground, will run out eventually.
Non renewable materials are non biodegradable, so they take much longer to break down.
cards.watch_out: Wood is only renewable if forests are managed and trees are replanted.
cards.grade9: Give two examples of each: renewable (wood, cotton); non renewable (metal ore, oil for plastics).

cards.title: System diagrams
cards.question: What are the parts of a system diagram, and what is the difference between open and closed loop systems?
points: A system diagram explains the parts of a circuit: input, process, output.

Input block: detects a signal from outside the system, such as a switch. Process block: receives the signal and decides what to do. Output block: turned on or off by the process, producing light, movement or sound.
Open loop system: only input, process and output. Example: a USB lamp.
Closed loop system: uses feedback to correct itself. Example: a thermostat keeps the temperature set.

example.heading: Lamp system diagram
lines: Input: plug the USB into a port
Process: the circuit flows with electricity
Output: the lamp light turns on

cards.watch_out: Only closed loop systems have feedback. A simple lamp has none, so it is open loop.
cards.hook: IPO, and closed loops talk back.
cards.grade9: Draw and label the feedback arrow from output back to input in a closed loop diagram.

cards.title: Soldering safely
cards.question: What equipment is used for soldering, and what does a good solder joint look like?
points: Soldering iron: melts solder. Hold it by the handle only; the tip reaches about 250 °C.
Soldering iron stand: holds the iron safely. Sponge: wipes excess solder off the tip.
Solder wire: when melted it joins wires to the printed circuit board (PCB) so electricity can flow.
A good joint has smooth, even edges and connects both the wire and the circuit board.
cards.watch_out: Too much solder, or solder touching only the wire or only the board, means the circuit will not work properly.
cards.grade9: Explain why a joint touching two wires is a problem: it creates the wrong connection (a short circuit).

cards.title: ACCESS FM
cards.question: What does ACCESS FM stand for, and how is it used?
points: Aesthetics: how the product looks and feels. Cost: the overall cost including materials.
Customer: who the intended buyer is. Environment: the product's effect on the environment.
Safety: precautions when making and using the product. Size: height, width, length and volume.
Function: the product's intended use. Materials: what the product is made from.
cards.watch_out: Use ACCESS FM to analyse an existing product or write a specification, not only as a list to memorise.
cards.hook: ACCESS FM: Aesthetics, Cost, Customer, Environment, Safety, Size, Function, Materials.
cards.grade9: Write one specific point for each letter about a product, such as Size: the lamp must fit on a bedside table, no taller than 300 mm.

cards.title: Textiles: fibres, yarns and fabrics
cards.question: What are natural and synthetic fibres, yarns, textiles and looms?
points: A fibre is a fine, hair-like structure. A yarn is made of many fibres twisted together, used for stitching or knitting.
Natural fibres come from plants or animals: cotton, wool, silk, linen.
Synthetic fibres are made from oil, coal and petrochemicals: polyester, acrylic, polyamide.
Textile describes fibre-based materials including fabrics. A loom is a machine that weaves yarns together to make fabric.
cards.watch_out: Fibre, yarn, fabric: small to big. Do not mix up fibre and yarn.
cards.hook: Fibre to yarn to fabric: hair, thread, cloth.
cards.grade9: Explain the environmental impact of synthetic fibres: made from oil (non renewable), and they shed microplastics when washed.

cards.title: Isometric drawing
cards.question: How do you draw a letter of the alphabet in isometric?
points: Isometric drawing shows a 3D object with three faces visible.
Vertical lines stay vertical. Horizontal edges are drawn at 30 degrees to the horizontal, going left and right.
Use isometric grid paper or a 30 degree set square and a ruler.
Draw the front face of the letter first, then project the depth back at 30 degrees, then join the back edges.

example.heading: Steps for the letter L
lines: Draw the L shape along the 30 degree lines on the grid
Draw short lines back from each corner to show depth
Join the ends, then rub out hidden lines and go over the outline

cards.watch_out: There are no horizontal lines in isometric drawing. Every non vertical line is at 30 degrees.
cards.hook: Up stays up; everything else at 30.
cards.grade9: Add tone: shade the top face lightest, one side medium and the other side darkest so it looks solid.

cards.title: Sarah Graham and realistic painting
cards.question: What is Sarah Graham known for, and how can you work in her style?
points: Sarah Graham is a British artist known for large, highly realistic (photorealistic) paintings of sweets, lollipops and toys.
She paints in oil on large canvases. Her compositions are close up and cropped, often with the subject in focus and the background blurred.
She uses bright, vivid colours and a huge range of tones, with strong highlights and reflections to make shiny wrappers look real.
To work in her style: work from a photo, use a grid to scale it up, blend colours smoothly and add white highlights last.
cards.watch_out: Realism depends on tone, not outlines. Look for the darkest darks and the brightest highlights.
cards.grade9: Explain the effect of the scale: making small sweets huge makes everyday objects feel exciting and important.

cards.title: The formal elements of art
cards.question: What are the formal elements you use to describe and make art?
points: Line, shape, form (3D shape), tone (light and dark), colour, texture, pattern and composition.
Tone makes objects look 3D. Use a range from light to dark.
Colour: primary colours (red, yellow, blue) mix to make secondary colours (orange, green, purple).
Composition is how everything is arranged in the artwork.
cards.watch_out: Use these words when you write about an artist. They show you understand how the art works.
cards.hook: Line, Shape, Form, Tone, Colour, Texture, Pattern: Lucy Sings For Ten Cats Twice Per day.
cards.grade9: Analyse an artwork in three steps: what you see, how the artist made it, and why you think they made those choices.

cards.title: Key terms checklist
cards.question: Can you define each key term from the knowledge organiser?
points: 6 Rs: reduce, reuse, recycle, refuse, repair, rethink.
Original source, manufacture, disposal. Needs, wants, design brief, client profile.
Hardwood (deciduous), softwood (coniferous), manufactured board. Renewable, non renewable.
Input, process, output, signal, open loop, closed loop. Soldering iron, stand, sponge, solder.
ACCESS FM. Fibre, yarn, textile, loom. Isometric: verticals and 30 degree lines.
cards.watch_out: The knowledge organiser gives example exam questions. Practise answering each with a definition plus an example.

written.q: Explain two of the 6 Rs, giving an example for each.
model: Names and defines one R, such as reuse: another use before throwing away (1)
Example, such as a food tin as a pen pot (1)
Names and defines a second R, such as repair: mending instead of throwing away (1)
Example, such as repairing a phone (1)

written.q: Draw and label a system diagram for a thermostat. Explain why it is a closed loop system.
model: Process: thermostat connects to the boiler (1)
Feedback keeps the set temperature, so it is closed loop (1)

written.q: What is the difference between primary and secondary data? Give an example of each.
model: Primary data is gathered directly from the client (1)
Secondary data comes from another source, such as the internet or a book (1)

written.q: Draw the letter T in isometric on isometric paper.
model: Depth shown consistently on all parts of the letter (1)
Neat, ruled lines with hidden lines removed (1)

exam_tips.timing: 50 minutes in class. Do the knowledge questions first, then leave at least 15 minutes for the isometric drawing.
section_a: Learn each term on the knowledge organiser with its example.

section_a.Watch out for pairs: reuse and recycle, refuse and rethink, needs and wants, primary and secondary.

section_a: Hardwoods and softwoods are about tree type, not hardness.
section_b: Use a ruler and a sharp pencil for the isometric drawing.
Vertical lines stay vertical; everything else at 30 degrees.
Rub out construction lines and go over the final outline.
grade9: Explain how a design cuts material, energy or waste. A casing that can be repaired makes the product last longer.
Name the exact material and process, not just wood or plastic.
